newsitem.title: GERMANY: German experts weigh mass cull of British cattle.
newsitem.headline: German experts weigh mass cull of British cattle.

text.p: German experts met in Bonn on Wednesday to discuss proposals to slaughter about 10,000 cattle originating from Britain, after officials confirmed the first case of mad cow disease in a German-born animal.

Agriculture Minister Jochen Borchert said he supported the plan to cull around 3,000 British cattle and their 7,000 offspring to protect consumer confidence and he believed the experts from Germany's 16 regional states would agree.
"I assume we'll decide this afternoon that these risk cases will be slaughtered and destroyed so the consumer can continue to be sure that meat on the market here carries no risk," Borchert said.

The Galloway cow which sparked the latest scare was born in Germany in 1992 but was the calf of a Britsh-born cow. The rest of the herd, from a farm near the town of Hoexter in North-Rhine Westphalia, was slaughtered early on Wednesday.

"We must try to make consumer protection as secure as possible. We know that there is a danger from cattle which come from Britain and we have to minimise that danger," said Baerbel Hoehn, the agriculture minister of North-Rhine Westphalia.

The cow in question died in December last year but the Agriculture Ministry confirmed only on Tuesday that tests had proved it was infected with bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE) or mad cow disease.
The ministry also said tests ruled out any possibility the cow had been fed with contaminated animal feed, leaving only the possibility that it had been infected by its mother.

Scientists have so far found no proof BSE can be passed down through generations but the news has prompted a frantic search for the animal's mother, with some reports saying it was in eastern Germany while others said it was in the Netherlands.
Officials also rushed to reassure consumers in Germany, who show a strong concern for public health matters.

"Our meat remains safe," said Konstantin Heeremann, the president of the German Farmers' Association, pointing out that Bonn had already imposed strict controls on British cows in Germany. "Galloway cows cannot be sold or brought to market."
Bonn took a tough stance last year after Britain admitted a likely link between BSE and its human equivalent, the deadly brain-wasting Creutzfeldt-Jakob Disease (CJD).
Germany was in the vanguard of countries that demanded -- and got -- a worldwide ban on British beef and its by-products.
It has refused to agree to any easing of the export ban, even passing its own legislation to block an EU decision allowing Britain to resume exports of bull semen.

The experts were also expected to discuss cattle of Swiss origin at their meeting on Wednesday. Switzerland has recorded the most cases of BSE after Britain, which has reported 165,000 cases in the last 10 years.
